title: Later reception was not a new Church decree
source_text: XXXVIII. Denique quod isti libri communi postea consensu recepti fuerunt, in causa non fuit novum quoddam Ecclesiae decretum, quo sancita fuerit eorum authoritas; sed quae in istis libris scrupulum quibusdam movebant paulatim lucem accipientibus, & probe intellectis, tandem desierunt esse qui dubitarent, & concesserunt omnes in sententiam priscorum Patrum, qui Apostolis proximi, hos libros tanquam ab iis acceptos posteris commendârunt: & frequenti usu atque lectione comprobarunt. Et certe quod istud non sit tribuendum Synodo Laodicenae, aut tertiae Carthaginiensi, patet, quia Synodi illae provinciales fuerunt, nec poterant, ex ipsa adversariorum sententia, fidem proprie obligare. Et revera de istis libris post Synodum Laodicenam dubitatum adhuc fuit. Nam tempore Hieronymi, qui fuit illa recentior, erant adhuc qui dubitarent. Praesertim vero manifestum est, nec Synodum Carthaginiensem, nec Decreta PP. Gelasii & Innocentii, sustulisse dubitationem circa Veteris Testamenti libros, quos Canonicos illi, nos Apocryphos putamus: quandoquidem usque ad Concilii Tridentini tempora, plurimi fuerunt, in ipsa Ecclesia Romana, qui librorum istorum authoritatem rejecerunt.
pass_a_gloss: Finally, that those books were afterward received by common consent — the cause was not some new decree of the Church by which their authority was sanctioned; but the things in those books which moved scruple for some, as they gradually received light and were rightly understood, at last those who doubted ceased to be, and all conceded to the opinion of the ancient Fathers who, nearest to the Apostles, recommended these books to posterity as received from them, and confirmed them by frequent use and reading. And certainly that this is not to be attributed to the Synod of Laodicea, or to the third Carthaginian, is plain, because those Synods were provincial, and could not, on the adversaries' own view, properly bind the faith. And in truth concerning those books there was still doubt after the Synod of Laodicea. For in the time of Jerome, who was later than that [synod], there were still those who doubted. But especially it is manifest that neither the Carthaginian Synod nor the Decrees of Popes Gelasius and Innocent removed the doubt concerning the Old Testament books which they hold Canonical and we hold Apocryphal: since right up to the times of the Council of Trent there were very many, in the Roman Church itself, who rejected the authority of those books.
pass_b_english: Finally, those books were later received by common consent — not because some new Church decree sanctioned their authority.

What had raised scruple in them gradually came into the light and was rightly understood; at last the doubters ceased, and all conceded to the ancient Fathers nearest the apostles, who recommended these books to later ages as received from them and confirmed them by frequent use and reading.
This cannot be credited to the Synod of Laodicea or the third council of Carthage: those synods were provincial, and on the adversaries' own view could not properly bind the faith.
In fact doubt about those books remained after Laodicea. In Jerome's day — later than that synod — some still doubted.

Above all, neither Carthage nor the decrees of Popes Gelasius and Innocent removed doubt about the Old Testament books they call canonical and we call apocryphal: right up to Trent, many inside the Roman Church itself rejected those books' authority.
